title: Across the Line of Control, Two Kashmirs Diverge Sharply
excerpt: India's Jammu and Kashmir is drawing record tourists and launching startups, while Pakistan-occupied Kashmir struggles with inflation, repression, and crumbling infrastructure.
body:
• Jammu and Kashmir recorded over 23 million tourist arrivals in 2024, with stone-pelting incidents dropping to zero and local militant recruitment at an all-time low
  • Pakistan-occupied Kashmir remains mired in political subjugation and infrastructure decay, with CPEC projects largely extracting resources rather than developing the region
  • The 2024 J&K Assembly elections saw 63% voter turnout, including first-time participation by West Pakistani Refugees who were denied voting rights for seven decades

A Developmental Fault Line

The Line of Control that divides Jammu and Kashmir from Pakistan-occupied territory has evolved well beyond its origins as a military frontier. According to a recent analysis in the Eurasia Review, the LoC now marks a developmental fault line — one side integrating into the global economy, the other trapped in what the report describes as a "political black hole."

Since India's abrogation of Article 370 in 2019, which stripped the region of its special constitutional status, Jammu and Kashmir has undergone what officials characterize as a structural transformation. District Development Council elections in 2020 and full legislative polls in 2024 restored representative governance, while welfare schemes including Ayushman Bharat and PM Kisan have been extended to every district.

Record Tourism, Zero Stone-Pelting

The numbers tell a striking story. Tourist footfall in J&K crossed 23 million in 2024, a record that would have seemed implausible a decade ago when the region was synonymous with shutdowns and security cordons. Stone-pelting, once a weekly occurrence funded by cross-border networks, has dropped to zero, according to security officials.

"Tourist footfall in J&K crossed 23 million in 2024, a record that would have seemed implausible a decade ago when the region was synonymous with shutdowns and security cordons."

Local recruitment into militant ranks has hit an all-time low. "The Kashmiri youth are no longer picking up guns; they are picking up laptops," the Eurasia Review report stated, pointing to startup incubators in Srinagar and industrial estates in Jammu as evidence of an economic pivot.

The 2024 Assembly elections provided what many analysts view as the definitive test. With 63% voter turnout, the results delivered what the report called "a public funeral for the Pakistan-sponsored narrative that Kashmiris reject Indian democracy." Women, youth, and marginalized communities including West Pakistani Refugees — denied voting rights for 70 years under Article 370 — exercised their franchise for the first time as equal citizens.

Across the LoC: Extraction and Stagnation

The contrast with Pakistan-occupied Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan could hardly be starker. Reports from India Narrative and IANS describe territories caught in cycles of political subjugation and infrastructural decay, where questioning forced accession to Pakistan remains a punishable offence.

The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, often presented as a transformative development project, has largely functioned as a resource extraction mechanism in the occupied territories, according to multiple analyses. Infrastructure benefits have flowed primarily to transit corridors rather than local communities.

Protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir have intensified in recent years, with civilians facing military crackdowns. On the Indian side, a significant breakthrough was recorded in the construction of one of the region's most complex tunnel projects — a milestone that underscored the divergent trajectories playing out on either side of the LoC.

Strategic Implications

The widening development gap carries implications beyond the two territories. India has used the post-Article 370 transformation as a diplomatic tool, arguing that integration and democratic governance have delivered what decades of special status could not. Pakistan continues to raise the Kashmir issue at international forums, but the ground reality — measurable in tourist numbers, voter turnout, and declining violence — has shifted the evidentiary landscape.

For the Kashmiri diaspora spread across the globe, the divergence raises uncomfortable questions. Families split by the LoC increasingly inhabit different economic realities, with those on the Indian side benefiting from infrastructure investment and digital connectivity while relatives across the line contend with inflation, repression, and diminishing prospects.

The transformation is far from complete. Critics argue that the democratic gains remain fragile and that the heavy security apparatus in J&K has not been proportionally reduced. But the direction of travel, measured against the trajectory on the other side of the LoC, has become difficult to dispute.
nri_angle: For Kashmiri diaspora communities split by the LoC, the widening development gap raises urgent questions about the future of cross-border family ties and the region's political trajectory.
author: Diaspora Desk
